cards.text: Israel's long prayer to the LORD ends with a promise. In view of all of it, they'll make a binding agreement, put it in writing, and seal it with the names of their leaders, Levites and priests. Today, friend, the pens come out.

Nehemiah the governor, son of Hacaliah, tops the list of those who sealed the document, followed by the priests, the Levites and the leaders of the people, name after name after name. That's a longer list than the office birthday card, and NOBODY skipped it.

But the ones who sealed it aren't the only ones in. The rest of the people step up too: priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, and everyone who separated themselves from the people of the land.

cards.question: True or false: Along with the rest of the people, their wives and their sons and daughters who are able to understand join in too.
The rest of the people and their families join their noble brothers and make a sworn oath. What do they commit to?

answers.text: Follow the Law of God given through Moses
Rebuild the walls of every city in Judah
Send yearly gifts to the king of Persia

cards.text: They promise to carefully obey all of the LORD's commandments, ordinances and statutes. Then they get specific, and the first promise starts right at home with their families.

cards.question: First family promise: their daughters won't ___ the people of the land, and their sons won't either.

cards.text: Next up is the Sabbath: say the people of the land show up with merchandise or grain to sell on the Sabbath day. Friend, a big shiny sale right on the holy day is a temptation I can feel from HERE.

cards.question: The people of the land are selling grain on the Sabbath. What does Israel promise?

answers.text: They won't buy from them that day
They'll buy only what they need
They'll trade goods instead of paying

cards.question: One more promise in that same breath. True or false: Every seventh year, Israel will let the fields lie fallow and cancel every debt.

cards.text: Now the oath turns to money. Israel puts itself under an obligation to give a third of a shekel every year.

cards.question: Israel promises a third of a shekel every year. What's that money for?

answers.text: The service of the house of God
Taxes for the king of Persia

cards.text: That money covers the showbread, the grain offerings and burnt offerings, the Sabbaths, the New Moons and feasts, and the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel. That is one HARD-working third of a shekel.

cards.question: Israel casts lots among the priests, Levites and people. What are the lots for?

answers.text: Which families bring wood and when
Which men guard the city gates

cards.text: Year by year, they'll bring the firstfruits of their land and of every fruit tree to the house of the LORD. The FIRST, friend, not the leftovers, and not the one that rolled under the counter.

cards.question: True or false: Israel promises to bring the firstborn of their sons and their livestock, as it is written in the Law.

cards.text: They'll also bring the priests the firstfruits of their grain offerings, their trees, their new wine and oil, AND their dough. DOUGH, friend, now somebody's speaking my language!

cards.question: A tenth of Israel's produce belongs to the ___, and it's collected in all the towns where the people work.

cards.text: When the Levites go out to collect that tenth, they don't go alone. A priest of Aaron's line goes along with them.

cards.question: When the Levites collect the tithes, they bring a ___ of the tithes to the ___ in the house of God.
The grain, new wine and oil all go to the storerooms where the priests, gatekeepers and singers stay. What's the big promise that wraps up Israel's oath?

answers.text: They won't neglect the house of their God
They'll build their God a bigger house

cards.text: That's the whole oath, start to finish, and it ends right at the house of God. Stick around, friend, because this story is NOT done.

findings.problem: The card cites only Nehemiah 10:29, but its last sentence ('the first promise starts right at home with their families') uses the content of 10:30, the promise about sons and daughters marrying. The citation is narrower than what the card tells.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The question opens with 'First family promise: their daughters won't ___' and never says whose daughters. 'Their' points back to the people named on earlier cards, which are no longer on screen.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The card says the money covers 'the Sabbaths.' Nehemiah 10:33 says it covers 'the Sabbath offerings.' The money pays for the offerings, not the Sabbaths themselves.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The wrong answers 'singers' and 'gatekeepers' are close enough to the right answer that a baker could argue for them. Nehemiah 10:39 puts the contributions in the storerooms where the singers and gatekeepers stay. Later in the same book (Nehemiah 13:5), the tithes of grain, new wine and oil are described as prescribed for the Levites, singers and gatekeepers.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The line saying the story isn't over ('Stick around, friend, because this story is NOT done.') is nearly the doc's own example ('Trust me, friend, this story's not done.'). It should be an original line.

rule.text: The examples show the idea. Write your own line each time.

findings.problem: All three true or false cards (stop 1 card 4, stop 1 card 10, stop 2 card 6) have True as the answer. A baker who notices this can answer them without reasoning. The docs ban patterns in question type and order, but they say nothing about balancing True and False answers across a walkthrough.
findings.question: Should true or false cards in a walkthrough mix True and False answers, so that 'always True' doesn't become a pattern a baker can guess from?

findings.problem: Nehemiah 10:32-39 is mostly a list of temple contributions: the shekel, the offerings, the wood, firstfruits, firstborn and tithes. 'Rules for offerings and feasts' is listed as a long stretch, which gets one summary story card, no choice cards and no stop of its own. But these verses are also the quoted covenant oath, the heart of the passage, and 'speeches' are listed as not a long stretch. Stop 2 treats the section as a speech, with a full stop of choice cards.
findings.question: When a passage's central event is a quoted covenant or oath made up of offering and contribution rules (like Nehemiah 10:32-39), should it count as a speech and get full story and choice cards, or as a long stretch of offering rules summed up in one story card?
